title: A Safety Net for Kids with Disabilities Is Getting Thinner
summary:
Imagine you use a wheelchair, and you want to join your school's cheerleading team. Your mom asks the school to help make that possible. When the school says no, where do you go?

For 46 years, families could turn to the Office for Civil Rights, or OCR. It is a small government office inside the Department of Education. Its job is to make sure schools do not treat students unfairly because of a disability, race, or religion.

In March 2025, the government cut nearly half of the Education Department's workers. Seven of the OCR's 12 regional offices closed — in cities like Atlanta, Chicago, Dallas, and San Francisco. The office now has 446 staff members.

Here is the big number: from March to September 2025, the office got more than 9,000 new complaints. It said it "resolved" over 7,000. But the GAO, a government watchdog, found that about 90% of those were simply thrown out, not investigated.

Liz Piñón is a mom in Crowley, Texas. Her daughter Felicita, an eighth grader who uses a power wheelchair, was told she could not join a cheerleading team. Piñón filed a complaint. It was rejected in July 2024.

Education Secretary Linda McMahon says the cuts bring "accountability" and "efficiency." Advocates worry families now have nowhere to turn.
why_it_matters: If a school ever says no to a kid who needs extra help because of a disability, families need somewhere to ask for a fair check — and this story is about that safety net getting thinner.

background_read: In the United States, laws like the Americans with Disabilities Act, passed in 1990, say that schools and other public places must give people with disabilities the same chances as everyone else.
The Department of Education is the part of the U.S. government that watches over schools, and the Office for Civil Rights inside it is the team that checks whether schools follow those fairness laws.
The GAO is the Government Accountability Office — a team that checks how the government spends money and whether it does what it promises, like a referee for the government.
Article_Structure: WHO: Students with disabilities and their families, the Office for Civil Rights (OCR) inside the Department of Education, Education Secretary Linda McMahon, and mom Liz Piñón with her daughter Felicita in Crowley, Texas.

WHAT: In March 2025 nearly half of the Education Department's workers were cut and 7 of the OCR's 12 regional offices closed; the office then got more than 9,000 new complaints, but the GAO found about 90% of the cases it called 'resolved' were simply thrown out.
WHERE: Across the United States — OCR regional offices closed in cities including Atlanta, Chicago, Dallas and San Francisco, and the Piñón family's complaint came from Crowley, Texas.
WHY: The office that is supposed to check whether schools treat students fairly now has far fewer staff and far fewer offices, so families who hear 'no' may have nowhere to turn.

perspectives.description: Education Secretary Linda McMahon says the cuts bring 'accountability' and 'efficiency', meaning she believes the department will work better with fewer workers.
Advocates worry that families like the Piñóns now have nowhere to turn when a school says no, because so few complaints are really investigated.
The GAO simply looked at the numbers without taking sides: more than 9,000 complaints came in, but about 90% of the ones called 'resolved' were thrown out instead of investigated.
